The research vessel Prometheus groaned as its landing struts settled into the marshy terrain of Kepler-442b. The planet's thick atmosphere pressed against the hull, making the ship's metal framework protest with sharp pings and low moans. It was an unwelcoming sound, two hundred light-years from the cramped cities of Earth.

Commander Henry Martin rolled out of his bunk, his body heavy under the planet's 1.3g gravity. He was a lean man in his early forties, with the kind of weathered face that came from years managing impossible missions. The burden of Earth's desperate gamble had carved deep lines around his eyes. He shuffled toward the control room, already dreading the coffee.

Dr. Kara Perry glanced up from her console, tucking a strand of red hair behind her ear. "Morning, Henry. You look terrible."

"Thanks." He poured himself a cup of the bitter synthetic brew. "Anything new overnight?"

"The luminescent spheres—we're calling them 'orbs' now—had another gathering about three klicks north. They dispersed at dawn. And our two junior researchers snuck out again. Bruno tracked them but lost their signal in the fog. I've been running a beacon to guide them back."

Henry cursed under his breath. Earth's biotech programs were so desperate for field researchers that they were sending kids barely out of secondary school. The two assigned to his mission, Jordan Martinez and Stella Ahmed, seemed to have no survival instinct whatsoever.

Not that there was obvious danger here. The orbs appeared harmless, just curious. The local fauna were docile herbivores—strange six-legged creatures that looked like a nightmare fusion of mammals and arthropods. Nothing had shown aggression.

But something had happened to Dr. Chen's expedition twelve years ago, and to the follow-up mission under Captain Reeves five years back.

He moved to the viewport. The planet's sun was rising somewhere above the perpetual cloud cover, turning the thick fog from black to grey. In the distance, the yellow-green canopy of the scrub forest was barely visible. Shapes moved among the undergrowth—probably a herd of the native grazers. Through the haze, details were impossible to make out. Even the deep ravine where they'd discovered Reeves' deliberately buried ship was completely obscured.

Three of the orbs were hovering over the grazing animals now, pulsing with soft bioluminescence. Henry stared at them, trying to understand their purpose. If he had time to study them properly...

But there was no time.

Earth's Global Migration Authority had ordered him to check this site after delivering his cargo of colonists to Stonegate Territory on World-designate Clinton Province. He'd already overstayed by ten days. If there was no explanation within another forty-eight hours for what happened to the researchers who'd abandoned their ship and equipment, he'd have to report back and recommend the planet be marked as hostile.

He would have left already, except a recent landslide had exposed enough of Reeves' ship for their metal detectors to catch it from aerial survey. It had been buried deep enough to fool the original search.

"Henry!" Kara's voice was sharp. "Henry, there are the kids!"

Before he could turn to her pointing finger, movement caught his peripheral vision.

The orbs had abandoned the herd. Now all three were racing at incredible speed toward a spot near the ship, hovering excitedly above something in the fog.

He saw the two researchers then, running back toward the Prometheus, just beyond the disturbance in the mist.

Something was emerging from lower ground. The fog swirled and parted. Henry grabbed the radio microphone, shouting a warning to the researchers.

They must have seen it the same moment his call reached them. Jordan grabbed Stella's arm and they spun around together.

Then the fog cleared completely.

Under the dancing orbs, a group of figures was advancing toward the researchers. Bipedal forms, roughly humanoid but wrong in every detail. One stood nearly seven feet tall, leading the others in a direct line toward the two young people in their environment suits. Some carried tools or weapons. The leader raised one arm—the gesture was unmistakably a command.

"Get the rovers out!" Henry yelled at Kara. He yanked open the officers' lift and hammered the descent button. The lift crawled downward with agonizing slowness. He burst out at the vehicle bay. Crew members were scrambling in confusion, but someone—one of the engineers—was taking charge. The rovers were lining up. The lead vehicle was already running, and Henry sprinted for it as the exit ramp deployed.

No time for full environment suits. The air here was breathable, if unpleasant—high in sulfur compounds and low in oxygen. He jumped into the passenger seat and saw that Dr. Bruno Singh was driving. At Henry's nod, the rover rolled down the ramp, its electric motors whining as it accelerated. Two more rovers followed.

The researchers had disappeared into the fog. Then Henry spotted them, surrounded by the humanoid figures. Up close, the beings looked grotesque—distorted proportions, covered in coarse hair, faces that suggested human features filtered through some alien lens.

The tall leader suddenly gestured toward the approaching rovers. He made an impossible leap backward, covering twenty feet. Others turned, two of them seizing the researchers. The rover was doing forty kilometers per hour, but the group began pulling away, despite carrying their captives. They descended into a depression, vanishing into the mist.

"Follow the orbs," Henry commanded. He regretted not wearing his suit—the radio would have let him coordinate with the other rovers. Too late now.

The orbs pursued the humanoids. Bruno drove the rover down into a gully with remarkable skill, but had to slow as the fog thickened. Then it cleared to reveal the group had doubled back to confuse pursuit.

No time to stop. The rover plowed through them. Henry glimpsed five-foot bodies diving aside. Faces covered in thick hair, eyes that seemed almost human. A spear clattered against the windshield from behind—the point was beautifully worked stone, impossibly sharp.

The humanoids vanished as Bruno fought to turn. The other rovers were catching up, but too late to help intercept. They had to reach the group holding the researchers before they all disappeared into the broken terrain.

An orb descended, nearly touching Henry's head. He raised his hand instinctively. There was a tingling sensation as the orb seemed to flow around his fingers. It rose a few inches and drifted away.

Suddenly, Bruno slammed the brakes. Henry lurched forward against his restraint. The seven-foot leader was standing directly ahead, a researcher on each shoulder.

The wheels locked and the rover skidded forward. The humanoid leaped back, dropping both researchers with a surprised grunt.

Henry was out before the rover stopped, diving at the figure. It had thin, elongated arms below massively developed shoulders, but incredible strength. Henry felt those arms wrench at him as his hands found the thick neck. An overwhelming stench filled his nostrils as the being fell backward. Bruno hit it a second after Henry's tackle. Its head struck rocky ground with a heavy thud, and it went limp, though still breathing.

Another rover arrived. Crew members were checking the researchers—both unharmed, Stella laughing or crying, Jordan trying to kick the unconscious humanoid. The two were loaded into one rover while others helped Bruno and Henry secure the captive before heading back.

"No skull fracture. Incredibly dense bone structure," Bruno said, shaking his head. "Remarkable physiology."

"I hope it survives," Henry told him. "You're assigned to keep it alive and conscious. Find out if it can communicate—signs, drawings, anything. I need to know what happened to Chen and Reeves, and why that ship was buried. This thing might have answers."

Bruno nodded grimly. "I'll try, though I can't risk pharmaceutical intervention on an unknown metabolism." He pulled out a cigarette, then grimaced. "Henry, none of this makes sense. We've surveyed this planet with thermal imaging—no settlements, no infrastructure, no signs of organized culture. We should have found something."

"Cave dwellers, maybe," Henry suggested. "Just call me when you learn anything. We need to get back to Earth. We're already past our window."

The researchers' reports were straightforward—they'd been grabbed and carried, but not harmed. Now they were enjoying their moment of drama. Henry confined them to quarters, knowing their accounts would only grow more embellished with each retelling.

If they could communicate with the captive, they might learn more than they could from excavating Reeves' ship. That vessel was probably stripped clean by now. The only logical conclusion was that both expeditions had been overcome by these humanoids.

But it raised troubling questions. How could primitives breach Reeves' ship? Why was the fuel dumped? Only trained personnel would know how to do that. And who taught these beings that a ship's metal detectors could be fooled by enough rock? They'd buried it with sophisticated understanding of human technology.

Maybe there would never be complete answers, but he had to find something—and quickly. Earth needed every marginally habitable world. The planet was dying, not from war or disaster, but from success. Twelve billion people, resources exhausted, ecosystems collapsed. Humanity had to spread to the stars or face extinction through slow suffocation on an overcrowded homeworld.

The race had survived its nuclear age, prevented interplanetary conflicts, developed faster-than-light travel, and found dozens of worlds that could—with massive terraforming—support human life.

But none were perfect. None were Earth. The explorers went out in desperation. The biotech teams did what they could with genetic engineering and environmental conservation. And the great colony ships began filling worlds with desperate volunteers.

Nearly seventy worlds now. The nearest a three-month journey from Earth and three months back.

If this world could be used, it would be among the closest. If not, no more time could be wasted here.

Primitives could be displaced, perhaps. It would be ruthless and morally questionable to take their world, but survival was the first law.

But how could primitives do what these had apparently done?

He studied the recovered spear. The shaft was laminated from strips of the local scrub wood, expertly crafted. The point was delicately knapped flint, done with a skill that modern humans had lost centuries ago.

"Beautiful primitive work," he muttered.

Kara pulled her coffee away from her lips and snorted. "You can see more of it outside."

He returned to the viewport. About fifty of the humanoids were squatting in the clearing fog, holding spears and staring at the ship. They waited perhaps eight hundred meters away. Waiting patiently. For what? The return of their leader? Or for an opportunity to take the ship?

Henry grabbed the comm and called Bruno. "Status on the captive?"

Bruno's voice sounded strange. "Physically stable. You should come down. But—"

Henry dropped the comm and headed for the medical bay. He cursed Bruno for not calling immediately, then cursed himself for not checking sooner. Then he stopped at the sound of voices.

Bruno was asking a question. A thick, harsh vocalization answered—a sound that made Henry's skin crawl. Bruno seemed to understand, responding as Henry entered.

The captive was sitting on the examination table, unrestrained and somehow unthreatening now. The heavy features were relaxed but focused. It made a gesture like a salute when it saw Henry enter, its eyes fixing on the insignia on his uniform.

"Haaroo, Commmaander," it said.

"Commander Martin, meet your predecessor, Commander Chen," Bruno said. His smile was forced, his face pale with strain.

The being nodded slowly and pulled something from the thick hair on its head. A tarnished silver eagle—a commander's insignia.

"He didn't mean to frighten the researchers—just wanted to talk," Bruno said quickly. "I've got some of the story. He's changed. Speech is difficult. They've had to modify language to fit their new vocal structures, and he's forgotten most standard English. But it gets easier. It's really Chen. I'm certain."

Henry had his doubts. An alien could have taken the insignia from a captured human, learned some words. But Chen had been his mentor.

"What was your daughter's name? What was your wife's profession? What was your research focus?"

The lips contorted into something like a smile, and the strangely proportioned fingers spread out.

"Maaree. Daaata anaalysis. Cuuultural sociooology."

The answers were correct.

By the time Chen finished his story, Henry and Bruno sat in stunned silence. Finally Henry stood. "Is it possible, Bruno?"

"No," Bruno said flatly. "Not by any biology I know. But it happened. I've examined tissue samples. The cellular changes are there. Hard to believe about their offspring. Mature in six years, but smaller. It shouldn't be hereditary—somatic changes don't alter germ cells. But in this case, the mechanism that changed Chen is real, so maybe the inheritance is equally real."

Henry escorted Chen to the exit. The waiting orbs descended to touch the transformed man, then leaped up again. The crowd of humanoids moved forward toward their leader. A few were nearly as tall as Chen, but most stood around five feet.

The children of the original expedition.

Back in the control room, Henry found the fuel purge controls, entered the authorization codes, and activated the sequence. There was a hiss and gurgle as the ship's fuel tanks discharged their contents onto the ground, where no technology could recover it to power the ship again.

He'd have to tell the crew eventually, after organizing his explanation so they could accept it, however much they might resist. But first he had to tell Kara.

"It was the orbs," he summarized. "They seem fascinated by humans. They don't need anything from us, but they enjoy our presence. Chen doesn't understand why. They can modify our cells, adapt us. Before humans came, all life here had six legs. Now they're changing that, as we've seen.

"And they don't need physical contact to do it. We've all been outside the hull. The changes don't show yet—but we're altered. In another month, Earth food would kill us. We have to stay. We'll bury the ship deeper, and Earth won't find us. They can't risk a colony where three ships disappear, so we'll vanish. And they'll never know."

No one would know. Their children—strange children who matured in six years—would be primitive in three generations. Earth tools would be useless for their changed hands. Nothing from the ship would last. Books would be unreadable to their new eyes. Eventually, Earth wouldn't even be a memory.

Kara stared out the viewport at what would be her home. Then she sighed. "You'll need to practice your presentation, but the others don't know you like I do, Henry. We can make them believe it. And it's too late now. But we haven't actually been changed yet, have we?"

"No," he admitted. Damn his voice—he'd never been good at deception. "No. They have to touch us directly. I've been touched, but the others could still return."

She nodded. He waited for her anger, but saw only confusion. "Why?"

Then, before he could answer, understanding dawned on her face. "The spawning ground."

It was the only option. Earth needed places to plant humanity's seed, but no world except Earth could be trusted to preserve that seed across generations. Some colonies were already showing instability.

Here, though, the orbs had adapted humans to the alien world instead of humans having to terraform the entire planet. Here, humanity's strange children could grow, develop, and begin the long climb back to civilization. The technology would be lost temporarily. But perhaps some of humanity's cultural values would remain to make the next rise better.

"We're needed here," he told her, his voice pleading for understanding he couldn't fully give himself. "These people need genetic diversity to give the new race strength. The forty-eight people on this ship will provide that foundation. We can't return to Earth, where no one would believe or accept this—or allow us to come back. We have to stay."

She smiled and moved toward him, seeking his strength. "Be fruitful," she whispered. "Be fruitful and multiply and replenish a world."

"No," he told her. "Replenish the stars."

But she was no longer listening, and that part of his vision could wait.

Someday, their children would find their way back to space exploration, seeking other worlds. With the orbs to help them adapt, they could claim most worlds. The unchanged human spirit would drive them through all space, and the changing bodies would conquer worlds beyond counting.

Someday, the entire galaxy would be a spawning ground for the children of humanity.

The Conspiracy on Titan Station

By JAMES MacCREIGH

Revolution was brewing on Titan Station, and Thomas Silva held the secret that would make the uprising succeed or fail. Yet he could make no move, could favor no side—his memory was gone—he didn't know for whom he fought.

Silva's hand flicked to his waist and hung there, poised. His plasma pistol remained holstered.

The tall, silver-haired woman—Catherine Willis—smiled.

"You're right, Silva," she said. "I could blast you, too. Nobody would win that way, so let's leave the weapons where they are."

The muscles twitched in Thomas Silva's cheeks, but his voice, when it came, was controlled. "Don't think we're going to let this go," he said. "We'll take it up with Dixon tonight. We'll see whether you can cut me out!"

The silver-haired woman's smile faded. She stepped forward, one hand bracing her against the thrust of the fusion engines underneath, holding to the guide rail at the side of the transport's corridor.

She said, "Silva, Dixon is your boss, not mine. I'm a free agent; I work for myself. When we land on Titan Station tonight I'll be with you when you turn our—shall I say, our cargo?—over to him. And I'll collect my fair share of the proceeds. That's as far as it goes. I take no orders from him."

A heavy-set man in blue appeared at the end of the connecting corridor. He was moving fast, but stopped short when he saw the two people.

"Hey!" he said. "Course correction—get to your cabins." He seemed about to walk up to them, then reconsidered and hurried off. Neither person paid any attention.

Silva said, "Do I have to kill you?" It was only a question as he asked it, without threatening.

A muted alarm bell sounded through the P.A. speakers, signaling a one-minute warning. The silver-haired woman cocked her eyebrow.

"Not at all," she said. She took the measure of her slim, dark-haired opponent. Taller, heavier, older, she was still no more uncompromisingly belligerent than Silva, standing there. "Not at all," she repeated. "Just take your fifteen thousand and let it go at that. Don't make trouble. Leave Dixon out of our private argument."

"Damn you!" Silva flared. "I was promised seventy-five thousand. I need that money. Do you think—"

"Forget what I think," Willis said, her voice clipped and angry. "I don't care about fairness, Silva, except to myself. I've done all the work on this—I've supplied the goods. My price is set, a hundred and fifty thousand Earth credits. What Dixon promised you is no concern of mine. The fact is that, after I've taken my share, there's only fifteen thousand left. That's all you get!"

Silva stared at her a long second, then nodded abruptly. "I was right the first time," he said. "I'll have to kill you!"

Already his hand was streaking toward the grip of his plasma pistol, touching it, drawing it forth. But the silver-haired woman was faster. Her arms swept up and pinioned Silva, holding him impotent.

"Don't be a fool," she grated. "Silva—"

The P.A. speaker rattled, blared something unintelligible. Neither heard it. Silva lunged forward into the taller woman's grip, sliding down to the floor. The silver-haired woman grappled furiously to keep her hold on Thomas's gun arm, but Thomas was slipping away. Belatedly, Willis went for her own weapon.

She was too late. Silva's was out and leveled at her.

"Now will you listen to reason?" Silva panted. But he halted, and the muzzle of his weapon wavered. The floor swooped and surged beneath him as the thrust of the mighty jets was cut off. Suddenly there was no gravity. The two people, locked together, floated weightlessly out to the center of the corridor.

"Course correction!" gasped silver-haired Willis. "Good God!"

The ship had reached the midpoint of its flight. The bells had sounded, warning every soul on it to take shelter, to strap themselves in their pressure bunks against the deadly stress of acceleration as the ship reversed itself and began to slow its headlong plunge into Titan Station. But the two people had not heeded.

The small steering rockets flashed briefly. The combatants were thrust bruisingly against the side of the corridor as the rocket spun lazily on its axis. The side jets flared once more to halt the spin, when the one-eighty turn was completed, and they were battered against the opposite wall, still weightless, still clinging to each other, still struggling.

Then the main-drive bellowed into life again, and the ship began to battle against its own built-up acceleration. The corridor floor rose up with blinking speed to smite them—

And the lights went out in a burst of crashing pain for Thomas Silva.

Someone was talking to him. Silva tried to force an eye open to see who it was, and failed. Something damp and clinging was all about his face, obscuring his vision. But the voice filtered in.

"Open your mouth," it said. "Please, Thomas, open your mouth. You're all right. Just swallow this."

It was a man's voice. Silva was suddenly conscious that a man's firm hand was on his shoulder. He shook his head feebly.

The voice became more insistent. "Swallow this," it said. "It's only a stimulant, to help you throw off the shock of your—accident. You're all right, otherwise."

Obediently he opened his mouth, and choked on a warm, tingly liquid. He managed to swallow it, and lay quiet as deft hands did something to his face. Suddenly light filtered through his closed eyelids, and cool air stirred against his damp face.

He opened his eyes. A slight dark-haired man in white medical uniform was standing there. He stepped back a pace, a web of wet gauze bandage in his hands, looking at him.

"Hello," he whispered. "You—where am I?"

"In the medical bay," the medic said. "You got caught out when the ship changed course. Lucky you weren't hurt, Thomas. The woman you were with—the old, silver-haired one, Willis—wasn't so lucky. She was underneath when the jets went on. Severe spinal damage—internal bleeding. She died in the other room two hours ago."

Silva screwed his eyes tight together and grimaced. When he opened them again there was alertness and clarity in them—but there was also bafflement.

"Sir," he said, "who are you? Where am I?"

"Thomas!" There was shock and hurt in the tone of his voice. "I'm—don't you know me, Thomas?"

Silva shook his head confusedly. "I don't know anything," he said. "I—I don't even know my own name."

"Silva, Silva," a man's heavy voice said. "That won't wash. Don't play dumb on me."

"Silva?" he said. "Silva...." He swiveled his head and saw a dark, squat man frowning at him. "Who are you?" Thomas asked.

The dark man laughed. "Take your time, Silva," he said easily. "You'll remember me. My name's Dixon. I've been waiting here for you to wake up. We have some business matters to discuss."

The medic, still eyeing Silva with an odd bewilderment, said: "I'll leave you alone for a moment. Don't talk too much to him, Mr. Dixon. He's still suffering from shock."

"I won't," Dixon promised, grinning. Then, as the medic left the room, the smile dropped from his face.

"You play rough, Silva," he observed. "I thought you'd have trouble with Willis. I didn't think you'd find it necessary to put her out of the way so permanently. Well, no matter. If you had to kill her, it's no skin off my nose. Give me a release on the merchandise. I've got your money here."

Silva waved a hand and pushed himself dizzily erect, swinging his legs over the side of the high cot. A sheet had been thrown over him, but he was fully dressed. He examined his clothing with interest—gray tunic, gray leather spacer's boots. It was unfamiliar.

He shook his head in further confusion, and the motion burst within his skull, throbbing hotly. He closed his eyes until it subsided, trying to force his brain to operate, to explain to him where and what he was.

He looked at the man named Dixon.

"Nobody seems to believe me," he said, "but I really don't know what's going on. Things are moving too fast for me. Really, I—why, I don't even know my own name! My head—it hurts. I can't think clearly."

Dixon straightened, turned a darkly-suspicious look on Silva. "Don't play tricks on me," he said savagely. "I haven't time for them. I won't mince words with you. Give me a release on the cargo now, before I have to get rough. This is a lot more important to me than your life is."

"Go to hell," Silva said shortly. "I'm playing no tricks."

There was an instant's doubt in Dixon's eyes, then it flashed away. He bent closer, peered at Silva. "I almost think—" he began.

Then he shook his head. "No," he said. "You're lying all right. You killed Willis to get her share—and now you're trying to hold me up. That's your last chance that just went by, Silva. From now on, I'm running this show!"

He spun around and strode to the door, thrust it open. "Hawkins!" he bellowed. "Green!"

Two large, ugly men in field-gray uniforms, emblazoned with the crossed-hammers insignia of Titan Station's Security Force, came in, looking to Dixon for instructions.

"Silva here is resisting arrest," Dixon said. "Take him along. We'll fix up the charges later."

"You can't do that," Silva said wearily. "I'm sick. If you've got something against me, save it. Wait till my head clears. I'm sure I can explain—"

"Explain, hell." The dark man laughed. "If I wait, this ship will be blasting off for Europa within two hours. I'll wait—but so will the ship. It's not going anywhere till I give it clearance. I run Titan Station; I'll give the orders here!"

II

Whoever this man Dixon was, thought Silva, he was certainly a man of importance on Titan Station. As he had said, he gave the orders.

The crew of the rocket made no objection when Dixon and his men took Silva off without a word. Silva had thought the medic, who seemed a good enough sort, might have said something on his behalf. But he was out of sight as they left. A curt sentence to a gray-clad official on the landing pad where the rocket lay, and the man nodded and hurried off, to tell the rocket's captain that the ship was being refused clearance indefinitely.

A long, powerful ground vehicle slid up before them. Dixon got in front, while the two uniformed men shoved Silva into the back of the vehicle, climbed in beside him. Dixon gave a curt order, and the vehicle shot forward.

The driver, sitting beside Dixon, leaned forward and reached a hand under the dashboard. The high wail of a siren came instantly from the vehicle's roof, and what traffic was on the broad, straight highway into which they had turned pulled aside to let them race through.

Ahead lay the tall spires of a city. Graceful, hundreds of feet high, they seemed dreamlike yet somehow oddly familiar to Silva. Somewhere he had seen them before. He dragged deep into his mind, plumbing the cloudy, impenetrable haze that had settled on it, trying to bring forth the memories that he should have had. Amnesia, they called it; complete forgetting of the happenings of a lifetime. He'd heard of it—but never dreamed it could happen to him!

My name, it seems, is Thomas Silva, he thought. And they tell me that I killed a woman!

The thought was starkly incredible to him. A silver-haired woman, it had been; someone named Willis. He tried to remember.

Yes, there had been a silver-haired woman. And there had been an argument. Something to do with money, with a shipment of goods that Willis had supplied to Silva. There had even been talk of killing....

But—murder! Silva looked at his hands helplessly.

Dixon, up ahead, was turning around. He looked sharply at Silva, for a long second. An uncertainty clouded his eyes, and abruptly he looked forward again without speaking.

"Who's this man Dixon?" Silva whispered to the nearest guard.

The man stared at him. "Administrator Dixon," he said, "is the Council's deputy on Titan Station. You know—the Earth-Mars Council. They put Administrator Dixon here to—well, to administer for them."

"Council?" Silva asked, wrinkling his brow. He had heard something about a Council once, yes. But it was all so nebulous....

The other guard stirred, leaned over. "Shut up," he said heavily. "You'll have plenty of chance for talking later."

But the chance was a long time in coming. Silva found himself, an hour later, still in the barred room into which he'd been thrust. The guards had brought him there, at Dixon's order, and left him. That had been all.

This was not a regular jail, Silva realized. It was more like a governmental complex, something reflecting the architectural design principles of Earth's brutalist period, all concrete and angular lines. Silva wished for human companionship—particularly that of the medic. Of all the people he'd met since awakening in that hospital bed, only he seemed warm and human. The others were—brutal, deadly. It was too bad, Silva reflected, that he'd failed to remember him. He'd seemed hurt, and he had certainly known him by first name. But perhaps he would understand.

Silva sat down on a lumpy, sagging bed and buried his head in his hands. Dim ghosts of memory were wandering in his mind. He tried to conjure them into stronger relief, or to exorcise them entirely.

Somewhere, some time, a woman had said to him, "Dixon is secretly arming the Titan Station dissidents for revolt against the Council. He wants personal power—he's prepared to pay any price for it. He needs weapons, Earth weapons smuggled in through the Council patrol. If he can wipe out the Security Force garrison—those who are loyal to the Council, still, instead of to Dixon—he can sit back and laugh at any fleet Earth and Mars can send. Transports are clumsy in an atmosphere. They're helpless. And if he can arm enough of Titan Station's malcontents, he can't be stopped. That's why he'll pay for plasma rifles with their weight in platinum."

Silva could remember the scene clearly. Could almost see the sharp, aquiline face of the woman who had spoken to him. But there memory stopped.

A fugitive recollection raced through his mind. He halted it, dragged it back, pinned it down....

They had stopped in Queenstown Region, the spaceport on the outer rim of the Glendale colony in Aldoria, as if the settlement knows shame and wants to hide the rough and roaring dome city that nestles in one of the great craters. Silva remembered sitting in a low-ceilinged, smoke-heavy room, across the table from a tall woman with silver hair. Willis!

"Six thousand plasma rifles," the woman had said. "Latest government issue. Never mind how I got them; they're perfect. You know my price. Take it or leave it. And it's payable the minute we touch ground on Titan Station."

There had been a few minutes of haggling over terms, then a handshake and a drink from a thin-necked flagon of pale-yellow liquid fire.

He and the silver-haired woman had gone out then, made their way by unfrequented side streets to a great windowless building. Silva remembered the white-hot stars overhead, shining piercingly through the great transparent dome that kept the air in the sealed city of Queenstown Region, as they stood at the entrance of the warehouse and spoke in low tones to the man who answered their summons.

Then, inside. And they were looking at a huge chamber full of stacked fiber boxes—containing nothing but dehydrated agricultural products and mining tools, by the stencils they bore. Silva had turned to the silver-haired woman with a puzzled question—and the woman had laughed aloud.

She dragged one of the boxes down, ripped it open with the sharp point of a handling hook. Short-barreled, flare-mouthed guns rolled out, tumbling over the floor. Ten of them were in that one box, and hundreds of boxes all about. Silva picked one up, broke it, peered into the chamber where the tiny capsule of U-235 would explode with infinite violence when the trigger was pulled, spraying radiant death four thousand yards in the direction the gun was aimed....

And that memory ended.

Silva got up, stared at his haggard face in the cracked mirror over the bed. "They say I'm a killer," he thought. "Apparently I'm a gun-runner as well. Good lord—what am I not?"

His reflection—white, drawn face made all the more pallid by the dark hair that fell over it—stared back at him. There was no answer there. If only he could remember—

"All right, Silva." The deep voice of a guard came to him as the door swung open. "Stop making eyes at yourself."

Silva looked around. The guard beckoned. "Administrator Dixon wants to speak to you—now. Let's not keep the administrator waiting."

A long, narrow room, with a long carpet leading from the entrance up to a great heavy desk—that was Dixon's office. Silva felt a click in his memory as he entered. This was a deliberate application of political philosophy and systems thinking to urban planning—one of the ancient Earth dictators had employed just such a psychological trick to overawe those who came to beg favors of him. Mussolini, or some such name.

The trick failed to work. Silva had other things on his mind; he walked the forty-foot length of the room, designed to imbue him with a sense of his own unimportance, as steadily as he'd ever walked in the open air of his home planet.

Whichever planet that was.

The guard had remained just inside the door, at attention. Dixon waved him out.

"Here I am," said Silva. "What do you want?"

Dixon said, "I've had the ship inspected and what I want is on it. That saves your life, for now. But the cargo is in your name. I could take it by force, if I had to. I prefer not to." He picked up a paper, handed it to Silva. "In spite of your behavior, you can keep alive. You can even collect the money for the guns—Willis' share as well as your own. This is a release form, authorizing my men to take six hundred and thirty cases of dehydrated foods and drilling supplies from the hold of the Meridian—the ship you came on. Sign it, and we'll forget our argument. Only, sign it now and get it over with. I'm losing patience, Silva."

Silva said, without expression, "No."

Dark red flooded into Dixon's sallow face. His jaws bunched angrily and there was a ragged thread of incomplete control to his voice as he spoke.

"I'll have your neck for this, Silva," he said softly.

Silva looked at the man's eyes. Death was behind them, peeping out. Mentally he shrugged. What difference did it make?

"Give me the pen," he said shortly.

Dixon exhaled a deep breath. You could see the tension leave him, the mottled anger fade from his face and leave it without expression. He handed the paper to Silva without a word. He gave him a pen, watched him scrawl his name.

"That," he said, "is better." He paused a moment ruminatively. "It would have been better still if you'd not stalled me so long. I find that hard to forgive in my associates."

"The money," Thomas said. If he were playing a part—pretending he knew what he was doing—he might as well play it to the hilt. "When do I get it?"

Dixon picked up the paper and looked carefully at the signature. He creased it thoughtfully, stowed it in a pocket before answering.

"Naturally," he said, "there will have to be a revision of terms. I offered a hundred and sixty-five thousand Earth-credits. I would have paid it—but you made me angry. You'll have to pay for that."

Silva said, "I've paid already. I've been dragged from pillar to post by you. That's enough. Pay me what you owe me, if you want any more of the same goods!"

That was a shot in the dark—and it missed the mark.

Dixon's eyes widened. "You amaze me, Silva," he said. He rose and stepped around the desk, confronting Silva. "I almost think you really have lost your memory, Silva," he said. "Otherwise, surely you would know that this is all the rifles I need. With them I'll take whatever else I want!"

Silva said, "You're ready, then...."

He took time to think it over, but he knew that no thought was required. Already the hands that he had locked behind him were clenched, taut. Already the muscles of his legs were tensing.

"You're ready," he repeated. "You've armed the Titan Station dissidents—the worst elements on nine planets. You're set to betray the Council that gave you power here.... Well, that changes things. I can't let you do it!"

He hurled himself at Dixon, hands sweeping around to grapple for the dark man's throat. Dixon, off-balance, staggered backward. But his own hands were diving for the twin heat guns that hung at his waist.

Silva saw his danger, and reacted. His foot twisted around Dixon's ankle; his hands at the other's throat gripped tighter. He lunged forward, slamming the hard top of his head into the other's face, feeling flesh and cartilage give as Dixon's nose mashed flat. His own head pin-wheeled dizzily, agonizingly, as the jar revived the pain of his earlier accident.

But Dixon, unconscious already, tumbled back with Silva on top of him. His head made an audible, spine-chilling thud as it hit the carpeted floor.

Silva got up, retrieving the two heat guns, and stared at him.

"They tell me I killed Willis the same way," he thought. "I'm getting in a rut!"

But Dixon was not dead, though he was out as cold as the void beyond Pluto. The thick carpeting had saved him from a broken head.

Silva stepped over the unconscious man and looked around the room. It was furnished severely, to the point of barrenness. Two chairs before Dixon's ornate, bare-topped desk and one luxurious chair behind it; a tasseled bell cord within easy reach of Dixon's chair; the long carpet. That was all it contained.

The problem of getting out was serious, he saw. How could one—

III

Methodically he ransacked the drawers of Dixon's desk. Papers, a whole arsenal of hand guns, Titan Station currency by the bale, ominously black-covered notebooks with cryptic figures littering their pages—those were the contents. A coldly impersonal desk, without the familiar trivia most men accumulate. There was nothing, certainly, that would get him out of a building that so closely resembled a fortress.

He tumbled the things back into the drawers helter-skelter, turned Dixon over and searched his pockets. More money—the man must have had a fortune within reach at all times—and a few meaningless papers. Silva took the release he had signed and tore it to shreds. But that was only a gesture. When Dixon came to, unless Silva had managed to get away and accomplish something, the mere lack of written permission would not keep him from the rocket's lethal cargo!

When Dixon came to....

An idea bloomed in Silva's brain. He looked, then, at unconscious Dixon—and the idea withered again.

He had thought of forcing Dixon himself to front for him, at gun's point, in the conventional manner of escaping prisoners. But fist fights, fiction to the contrary notwithstanding, leave marks on the men who lose them. Dixon's throat was speckled with the livid marks of Silva's fingers; Silva's head, butting Dixon in the face, had drawn a thick stream of crimson from his nostrils, turned his sharp nose askew.

No guard of Dixon's would have been deceived for an instant, looking at that face—even assuming that Dixon could have been forced to cooperate by the threat of a gun. Which, considering the stake Dixon had in this play, was doubtful....

He stood up and looked around. He had to act quickly. Already Dixon's breath was audible; he saw the man grimace and an arm flopped spasmodically on the floor. Consciousness was on its way back.

Silva touched the heat gun he'd thrust into his belt; drew it and held it poised, while he sought to discover what was in his own mind. He'd killed a woman already, they said. Was he then a killer—could he shoot Dixon now, in cold blood, with so much to gain and nothing to lose?

This was ethical decision-making at its most stark. The question of social justice weighed on him—Dixon was planning to arm dissidents who would overthrow legitimate authority, plunging Titan Station into chaos. Yet Silva found himself unable to pull the trigger on an unconscious man.

He stood there a moment. Then, abruptly, he reversed the weapon and chopped it down on Dixon's skull.

There was a sharp grunt from the still unconscious man, but no other sign. Only—the first tremors of movement that had shown on him halted, and did not reappear.

"No," Silva thought. "Whatever they say, I'm not a killer!"

But still he had to get out. How?

Once more he stared around the room, catalogued its contents. The guard would be getting impatient. Perhaps any minute he would tap the door, first timorously, then with heavier strokes.

The guard! There was a way!

Silva eyed the length of the room. Forty feet—it would take him a couple of seconds to run it at full speed. Was that fast enough?

There was only one way to find out.

He walked around the desk to the bell cord. He took a deep breath, tugged it savagely, and at once was in speedy motion, racing toward the door, his footsteps muffled in the deep, springy carpet. Almost as he reached it, he saw it begin to open. He quickly sidestepped and was out of the guard's sight, behind the door, as the man looked in.

Quick suspicion flared in his eyes, then certainty as he saw Dixon huddled on the floor. He opened his mouth to cry out—

But Silva's arm was around his throat, and he had no breath to spare. Silva's foot lashed out and the door slammed shut; Silva's balled left fist came up and connected with the guard's chin. Abruptly the man slumped.

Silva took a deep breath and let the man drop to the floor. But he paused only a second; now he had two unconscious men on his hands and he dared let neither revive until he was prepared.

He grasped the guard's arm and dragged him roughly the length of the room. He leaped on top of the desk, brutally scarring its gleaming top with the hard spikes of his boots. His agile fingers unfastened the long bell cord without causing it to ring and, bearing it, he dropped again to the floor.

Tugging and straining, he got the limp form of Dixon into his own chair, bound him with the bell cord, gagged him with the priceless Venusian-silk scarf Dixon wore knotted about his throat. He tested his bindings with full strength, and smiled. Those would hold, let Dixon struggle as he would.

The guard he stripped of clothing, bound and gagged with his own belt and spacer's kerchief. He dragged him around behind the desk, thrust him under it out of sight. Dixon's chair he turned so that the unconscious face was averted from the door. Should anyone look in, then, the fact of Dixon's unconsciousness might not be noticed.

Then he took off his own clothes, quickly assumed the field-gray uniform of the guard. It fit like the skin of a fruit. He felt himself bulging out of it in a dozen places. The long cape the guard wore would conceal that, perhaps. In any case, there was nothing better.

Trying to make his stride as martial as possible, he walked down the long carpet to the door, opened it and stepped outside.

The corridor beyond was empty, stretching in both directions with the cold efficiency of bureaucratic architecture. Silva's heart pounded as he moved forward, trying to look purposeful, trying to remember which way they had brought him in. His mind, still clouded by amnesia, offered no help.

He chose left, walking with measured steps. Two other guards passed him, nodded curtly, continued on. He forced himself not to look back, not to betray his nervousness.

At the end of the corridor, a lift. He stepped inside, studied the panel. Twenty floors, and he was on the eighteenth. He pressed the button for the ground level and felt the lift descend smoothly.

When the doors opened, he stepped out into a vast lobby. People in civilian clothes moved about, conducting business. More guards stood at various posts. And there, across the expanse of polished floor, were the main doors leading outside.

Silva walked toward them, every nerve screaming at him to run. But he maintained his pace, kept his face impassive. A guard at the door nodded to him as he approached.

"Shift change already?" the guard asked.

Silva grunted noncommittally and kept walking. The guard shrugged and let him pass.

Outside, the artificial atmosphere of Titan Station pressed around him, the great dome overhead showing the swirling orange clouds of Saturn beyond. He was free—for now.

But free to do what? He still didn't know who he really was, what side he was truly on. The weapons were still on that ship, waiting to fuel a revolution that might be just or might be catastrophic. And somewhere in his locked memory was the key to everything.

Silva looked up at the dome, at Saturn's vast presence beyond, and wondered what he would do next. The only thing he knew for certain was that he had to find out the truth—about himself, about Dixon, about everything.

And he had to do it before those weapons were unloaded and Titan Station exploded into violence.
quality_problem.question: What role does Dixon hold on Titan Station?

VIRTUAL SHORES
By MARSHALL KING

Elena Wagner laughed as her avatar sprinted through the digital forest, her consciousness fully immersed in the simulation. At twelve years old, she had finally earned enough credits from her creative writing assignments to purchase a full day pass to the Greenfield Territory simulation—the most advanced virtual environment in Crestwood, Zelvaria. Today, she would finally explore the legendary Digital Ocean, a marvel of computational oceanography that her older siblings had described in breathtaking detail.

When she'd caught her breath, she checked her interface. No trace of the starting hub; she had left it far behind in the procedurally generated wilderness. Safe from the scrutiny of moderators and parental controls, there was nothing now to stop her from reaching the ocean. This was the moment to activate her special ability.

"On your mark!" she shouted to the flowing data streams that manifested as a rippling brook with orange whirlpools. She glanced around, pretending that some glitch might try to interrupt her. "Get set!" she challenged the algorithmic insects that hovered over the abundant foliage. "Pause!"

She activated her time-manipulation module—a rare power-up she'd won in a creative writing competition. The system responded instantly: the data stream became motionless and its minute whirlpools stopped whirling; a nearby digital bee hung suspended over a flowering plant, its wings frozen mid-stroke; and the purple sky overhead held fast in its generation of clouds and atmospheric effects.

With everything around her in a state of perfect stasis, Elena hurried toward the ocean. Her avatar moved through the frozen world with practiced ease.

If only the session wasn't time-limited! she thought. There was so much to see and her credits would only last six hours. It seemed that everyone except her had explored the beach country. The stories she had heard from her siblings and their friends had tantalized her for months. So many times had she heard these descriptions that now, as she ran along, she could clearly picture the wonderland as though she were already there. There would be a formation of petrified logs to climb on, the ocean itself with waves generated by the most sophisticated fluid dynamics algorithms in existence, the comical three-legged creatures called tripods who endlessly processed seaweed data, and many kinds of other procedural creatures found only at the ocean biome.

She bounded through the forest as though the virtual world was reserved this day just for her. And who could say it wasn't? she thought. Wasn't this her first solo expedition? She ran along feeling sorry for younger users who wouldn't dare venture to the ocean alone. But twelve!

"I'll unpause you, Mr. Bee—just wait and see!" As she passed one of the many motionless pollen-gathering subroutines, she took care not to disturb its interrupted task. When Elena had paused time, the bees—like all the other entities—had been frozen in their programmed activities, and she knew that as soon as she resumed time, everything would pick up exactly where it had left off.

When she detected the distinct sensory data that told her the ocean was not far off, her pulse quickened. Rather than spoil what was clearly going to be a perfect day, she chose to ignore the fact that using time-manipulation consumed enormous amounts of processing power and drained her avatar's energy reserves. She chose to ignore the warning that "young users who manipulate time without proper authorization may suffer permanent account suspension." She chose to ignore the cautionary tales about users who had exhausted their avatars and been forcibly disconnected.

She chose, instead, to picture the admiration of family and friends when they learned of her brave journey.

The journey was long, the clock stood still. She stopped to gather some fruit that grew along the path—nutritional data packets that would restore her avatar's stamina. With them in her inventory, she bounded along several more meters, then stopped abruptly.

She found herself atop a rocky promontory, overlooking the Digital Ocean!

She was so overwhelmed by the vista that her "Amazing!" came out as a weak whisper. The ocean lay before her, its paused waves awaiting her command to resume their tidal algorithms. The breakers along the shoreline hung in varying stages of formation, some having already exploded into towering spray while others were poised in smooth orange curls waiting to execute that subroutine.

And there were new entities everywhere! Overhead, a flock of seabirds were frozen in a steep glide, their flight paths calculated but suspended. Elena had heard of these interactive creatures many times. Today, with her siblings logged into their own sessions elsewhere, she would have the entities all to herself. Further down the beach was a pair of humanoid avatars frozen mid-step, facing the spot where Elena now stood. Some distance behind them were eight more, each frozen in curious poses. And down in the water, where the ocean algorithms ran themselves into thin pixels upon the sand, she saw the comical tripods, those three-legged marine entities who made careers of processing seaweed.

"Hi there!" Elena called. When she got no reaction, she remembered that she was still in time-manipulation mode. For her, the world would continue to be frozen until she resumed time.

"Hi there!" she called again, this time with the mental command to resume. Time started! Immediately she was surrounded by activity. She heard the roar of the crashing orange breakers, she experienced the spray's sensory data, and she saw her new companions continue their actions.

She knew, too, that at this moment, in the forest, the little brook picked up its flow where it had left off, the purple clouds resumed their programmed journey, and the bees continued their tasks without having missed a single wing-stroke. The brook, the clouds, and the insects had not been interrupted in the least; it was time itself that Elena had paused, not the simulation around her.

She scrambled down the sandy cliff to meet the tripods who, to her, had just come to life.

"I can do a handstand!" She set down her fruit and balanced herself upside down while her legs pawed the air. She knew it was probably the worst handstand she had ever done, for she felt weak and dizzy. Already time-manipulation had drained her avatar's energy. But her spirits remained high.

The tripod acknowledged Elena's feat with an appreciative animation before returning to its seaweed processing.

Elena ran everywhere, trying to see and do everything at once. She looked around to greet the flock of seabirds, but they had glided to a spot further along the shore. Then, approaching the first of the humanoid avatars, she started to burst forth with her habitual "Hi there!" when she heard them speaking.

"...will revolutionize market economics in virtual spaces, Patel. This simulation makes seventeen. Seventeen proprietary environments I can claim as my intellectual property!"

"My, my. Seventeen simulations. And tell me, Antonio, just what the hell are you going to do with them—display them in your digital portfolio back in Keystone, Belvoria?"

"Hi there, wanna explore together?" Elena's invitation got nothing more than a startled glance from the avatars who quickly returned to their conversation. She followed along at their heels. "I've got some fruit, want some?"

"Patel, you'd better tell your team back there to stop admiring the visual arts and get to work. Time is money. I didn't fund this media production expedition just to give your assistants a vacation."

The avatars stopped so suddenly that Elena nearly collided with them.

"All right, Antonio, just hold it a minute. Listen to me. Sure, it's your funding that created this place; it's your project all the way. But you hired me to lead the technical team here with the best programmers available, and that's just what I've done. My job isn't over yet. I'm responsible for documenting this environment safely, and for completing the data extraction."

"Precisely. And since you're responsible, get them working. Tell them to deploy the marker. Look at those fools back there, playing in the ocean with a three-legged algorithm!"

"Good God, man, aren't you human? We've only been in this simulation twenty minutes! Naturally they want to explore. They half expected to find hostile entities or worse, and here we are surrounded by friendly creatures that approach us like we're old friends. Let the team look around before we stake out your copyright claim."

"Bah! Bunch of children."

As Elena followed along, an avatar's leg swung at her and missed. "Patel, will you get this glitchy NPC away from me!" Elena shrieked with joy at this new interaction and promptly did a handstand. In this position she got an upside-down view of them walking away.

She gave up trying to stay with them. Why did they move so fast? What was the hurry? As she sat down and began consuming her fruit to restore energy, three more avatars came along making urgent sounds, apparently trying to catch up to the first two. As they passed her, she offered her fruit. "Want some?" No response.

Exploration held more promise than eating. She left her fruit half-consumed and went to where they had stopped further along the beach.

"Director Patel, sir! Isaac has detected anomalous code in the vicinity. He's trying to isolate it now."

"There you are, Antonio. Your new intellectual property is going to make you so wealthy that you can fund your next simulation. That'll make eighteen, I believe."

"Anomalous code, bah! We've found low-grade exploits in every environment I've developed so far, and this one'll be no different. Now how about that marker? Let's get it deployed, Patel. And the copyright beacon, and the ownership certificate."

"All right, team. The sooner we get Mr. Antonio's marker deployed and his claim established, the sooner we can take time to explore properly. Quickly now!"

When the three avatars went back to join the rest of their group, the first two resumed walking. Elena followed along.

"Well, Patel, you won't have to look far for materials to use for the base of the marker pole. Look at that formation up there."

"Can't use them. They're petrified logs. The ones on top are too high to access, and if we move those on the bottom, the whole structure will collapse on us."

"Well—that's your problem. Just remember, I want this marker to be permanent. It's got to be stable for at least—"

"Don't worry, Antonio, we'll get your monument erected. What's this with the marker? There must be more to establishing a copyright than just deploying a marker."

"There is, there is. Much more. I've fulfilled all requirements set down by digital property law to validate my claim. But the marker? Well, you might say it represents an empire, Patel. The Antonio Empire. On each of my markers is the name ANTONIO, a symbol of innovation and progress in media production. Call it branding if you will."

"Don't worry, I won't. I've seen corporate markers before."

"Damn it all, will you stop referring to this as a corporate land-grab? What I'm doing is significant, man. Significant! This is digital pioneering."

"Of course. And if I'm not mistaken, you've set up a licensing system so that you not only own the environments, but you will effectively control the users who are foolish enough to pay for access."

"I could terminate your contract for talking to me like this. Damn you, man! It's people like me who fund development. It's people like me who give your programmers something to build. It's people like me who invest capital into risky projects like this, so that people like you can escape from overcrowded server farms. Did you ever think of that?"

"I imagine you'll triple your investment in six months."

When they stopped, Elena stopped. At first she had been interested in their conversation about market economics and intellectual property, but as she grew accustomed to their presence, and as they in turn ignored her, she hopped alongside chattering to herself, content to be in their company.

She heard more voices coming from behind, and she turned to see the remainder of the group running toward them.

"Director Patel! Here's the marker, sir. And here's Isaac with the code scanner. He says the anomaly is getting stronger over this way!"

"How about that, Isaac?"

"This scanner's going wild, Director. It's almost off the charts."

Elena saw one of the avatars hovering around her with a small device. Grateful for the attention, she did a handstand. "Can you do this?" She was delighted at the reaction. They all started making excited sounds, and she felt most satisfied.

"Stand back, Director! Here's the source right here! This little avatar's radiating more anomalous code than a corrupted database!"

"Let me see that, Isaac. Well, I'll be damned! Now what do you suppose—"

By now they had formed a widening circle around her, and she was eager to show them more tricks. She gambled on standing on one leg.

"Patel, I must capture that entity! Put it in a containment field."

"Now wait a minute, Antonio. Universal Digital Rights Protocol forbids—"

"This is my simulation and I make the rules. Put it in a containment field!"

"With my team as witness, I officially protest—"

"Good God, what a specimen to extract. Anomalous entities! Why, they must be self-replicating, of course! There must be thousands of these glitches somewhere in the code. And to think of those fools back in Keystone with their standard debugging protocols! Hah! Now I'll have investors flocking to me. How about it, Patel—does innovation pay off or doesn't it?"

"Not so fast. Since this little entity is anomalous, there may be great danger to the system—"

"Now look here! You had planned to put code samples in a secure container, so what's the difference? Put it in a containment field."

"It'll corrupt."

"I have you under contract, Patel! You are responsible to me, and what's more, you are in my simulation. Put it in a containment field."

Elena was tired. First the time-manipulation, then this. While this day had brought more excitement than she could have hoped for, the strain was beginning to show. She lay in the center of the circle, happily exhausted, hoping that her companions would show her some of their own abilities.

She didn't have to wait long. The avatars forming the circle stepped back and made way for two others who came through carrying a glowing containment device. Elena sat up to watch.

"Hell, Director, why don't I just grab the entity? Looks like it has no intention of fleeing."

"Better not, Matthew. Even though you're protected, no telling what abilities the little thing has. Play it safe and use the capture beam."

"I swear it understands what we're saying. Look at those eyes."

"All right, careful now with that beam."

"Come on, little one. Here you go. That's it!"

Elena took in these sounds with perplexed concern. She sensed the imploring quality of the avatar with the device, but she didn't know what she was supposed to do. She tilted her head as she waited in anticipation.

She saw the beam projecting toward her, and, before she knew it, she had scooted out of the circle and up the sandy beach. She was surprised at herself for fleeing. Why had she done it? she wondered. Never before had she felt this instinctive urge to protect herself.

She watched the avatars huddle around the containment device on the beach, their attention apparently diverted. She wished now that she had not run away; she felt she had lost her chance to interact with them.

"Wait!" She ran over to her half-consumed fruit, picked it up, and ran back into the crowd. "I've got my fruit, want some?"

The group came to life once more. Her companions ran this way and that, and at last Elena understood that the objective was to get her into the containment field. She picked up the spirit of the game, and deliberately ran within a few feet of the device, then, just as the nearest pursuer was about to push her in, she sidestepped to safety. Then she heard a sharp sound and felt a stinging sensation in one of her legs.

"Antonio, you fool! Put away that deletion tool!"

"There you are, team. It's all in the technique. Just tagged it, that's all. Now capture it."

The sting in her leg was minor; Elena's distress lay in her confusion. What had she done wrong? When she saw the capture beam projecting toward her again, she involuntarily paused time. She knew better than to use this ability recklessly, but her action now was instinctive. In that split second following the sharp sting in her leg, her mind had grasped for an acceptable course of action. Finding none, it had ordered the pause.

The scene around her became frozen once more. The beam hung motionless in the air while energy particles traced their way back to one of the avatars. Elena dragged herself through the congregation, confused by her inability to understand.

As she worked her way past one entity after another, she tried at first to avoid looking them in the eye, for she felt sure she had violated some rule. Then she thought that by examining them as she passed, she might discover their purpose. She limped by one who held a small device that had been emitting particles; the particles now hung in lifeless clusters around the avatar's head. She hobbled by another who held a scanner that had previously made sounds whenever Elena was near. These things told her nothing.

Before starting her climb up the promontory, she passed a tripod which, true to its nature, was comical even in alarm. Startled by the deletion tool's discharge, it had jumped four feet into the air before Elena had paused time. Now it hung there, its data-processing appendage extended and its three legs drawn up.

Leaving the frozen figures behind, she limped her way up the promontory, torn between leaving and staying. What an odd place, this ocean simulation! She wondered why she had not heard more details about the beach avatars.

Reaching the top of the rise, she looked down upon her silent companions with deep sorrow. How she wished she were down there interacting with them. But she knew at last that theirs was a game she didn't fit into. Now there was nothing left but to resume time and start the long journey back to the hub. Even though her session time was nearly expired, she knew she didn't dare use time-manipulation to get herself back instantly. Her depleted energy reserves and clouded thoughts were strong signals that she had already overused this ability.

When Elena resumed time, the avatar with the capture beam stood in open-mouthed disbelief as the beam fell harmlessly to the sand—on the spot where Elena had been standing.

"My God, it's—it's gone."

Then another avatar, the one with the deletion tool, ran a few steps toward the beam, stopped and gaped. "All right, people, what's going on here? Capture that entity. What did you do with it?"

The resumption of time meant nothing at all to those on the beach, for to them time had never stopped. The only thing they could be certain of was that at one moment there had been a glitchy creature in front of them, and the next moment it was gone.

"Is it invisible, Director? Where is it?"

"Up there, Director! On those rocks. Isn't that it?"

"Well, I'll be damned!"

"Patel, I'm holding you personally responsible for this! Now that you've bungled it, I'll bring it down my own way."

"Just a minute, Antonio, let me think. There's something about that anomalous little entity that we should.... Antonio! I warned you about that tool!"

Elena moved across the top of the formation for a last look at her companions. Her weight on the end of the first log triggered the collapse. Slowly at first, the giant logs began cascading down the short distance to the sand. Elena fell back onto solid ground, horrified at the spectacle before her. The agonizing sounds of the avatars below filled her with panic.

The logs caught most of them as they stood in the surf. Others were pinned down on the sand.

"I didn't mean it!" Elena screamed. "I'm sorry! Can't you hear?" She hopped back and forth near the edge of the rise, overwhelmed with shock and guilt. "Get up! Please get up!" She was consumed with distress at the sounds reaching her ears from the beach. "You're getting submerged! Did you hear me? Please get up." She was choked with anguish. How could she have caused this? She wanted her companions to get up and tell her it was all right. But it was beyond her power to bring it about.

The rising tide threatened to cover those in the orange surf.

Elena worked her way down the hill, begging them to save themselves. The sounds they made carried a new tone, a desperate quality she'd never heard before.

"Matthew! Grace! Can you hear me?"

"I—I can't move, Director. My avatar, it's.... My God, we're going to drown!"

"Look around you, Grace. Can you see anyone moving?"

"The team on the beach are nearly buried, Director. And the rest of us here in the water—"

"Antonio. Can you see Antonio? Maybe he's—" The voice was cut off by a wave gently rolling over.

Elena could wait no longer. The tides were covering one of the avatars, and soon the others would be in the same situation. Disregarding the consequences, she ordered time to pause.

Wading into the surf, she worked a log off one victim, then she pulled the avatar up to the sand. Through blinding tears, Elena worked slowly and carefully. She knew there was no hurry—at least, not as far as her companions' safety was concerned. No matter what their condition was at this moment, it would remain the same until she resumed time. She made her way deeper into the orange liquid, where a raised hand signaled the location of a submerged body. The hand was clutching a large white banner that was tangled among the logs. Elena worked the avatar free and pulled it ashore.

It was the one who had been carrying the deletion tool.

Scarcely noticing her own damaged leg, she rescued one victim after another until there were no more in the surf. Up on the beach, she started removing the logs that pinned down the avatars caught there. She removed a log from one, who then remained in a sitting position, face frozen in a mask of shock. Another, with the weight removed, rolled over into a new position. Elena whimpered in misery as she surveyed the chaotic scene.

At last she could do no more; she felt consciousness slipping away from her.

She instinctively knew that if she lost consciousness during time-pause, events would resume... without her. For Elena, this would mean disconnection. If she had to lose consciousness, she knew she must first resume time.

Step by step she climbed the little hill, pausing every now and then to consider if this were the moment to resume time before it was too late. With her energy fast draining, she reached the top of the promontory, and she turned to look down once more on the group below.

Then she realized how much her avatar had suffered: when she ordered time to resume, nothing happened.

Her heart sank. She wasn't afraid of disconnection, and she knew that if she disconnected the oceans would flow again and her companions would move about. But she wanted to see them safe.

She tried to clear her mind for supreme effort. There was no urging time to start. She knew she couldn't initiate it by degrees, first slowly then fully. Time either progressed or it didn't. She had to commit completely.

Then, without knowing exactly when it happened, her mind took command....

Her companions came to life. The first one she saw stir lay face-down and pounded fists on the beach. A flood of relief settled over Elena as sounds came from the avatar.

"What's the matter with me? Somebody tell me! Am I glitching? Isaac! Robert! What's happening?"

"I'm coming, Matthew! Heaven help us—I saw it, too. We're either corrupted or those damn logs are sentient!"

"It's not the logs. How about us? How'd we get out of the water? Isaac, we're both corrupted."

"I'm telling you, it's the logs, or rocks or whatever they are. I was looking right at them. First they're on top of me, then they're piled up over there!"

"Damnit, the logs didn't pull us out of the ocean, did they? Director Patel!"

"Are you all right?"

"Yes sir, but—"

"Who saw exactly what happened?"

"I'm afraid we're not processing right, Director. Those logs—"

"I know, I know. Now compose yourselves. We've got to gather the others and exit this simulation while we still can."

"But what happened, Director?"

"Hell, Matthew, don't you think I'd like to know? Those logs are petrified code. The whole team couldn't lift one. It would take extraordinary processing power to move one of those things."

"I haven't seen anything extraordinary. Those tripods down there are so busy with their seaweed algorithms—"

"All right, let's help the others. Some of them can't walk. Where's Antonio?"

"He's sitting down there in the water, Director, laughing hysterically. Or crying. I can't tell which."

"We'll have to get him. Isaac, Robert, come along. Antonio! You all right?"

"Ha-ha-ha! Seventeen! Seventeen! Seventeen simulations, Patel, and they'll do anything I say! This one's got a mind of its own. Did you see that trick with the rocks? Ha-ha!"

"See if you can find his deletion tool, Robert; he'll either corrupt himself or one of us. Restrict his permissions and take him back to the exit portal. We'll be along shortly."

"Hee-hee! Seventeen! Patel, I'm holding you personally responsible for this. Ha-ha!"

Elena opened her eyes as consciousness returned. Had her companions gone?

She pulled herself along to a position between two rocks, where she could see without being seen. By the light of the twin moons she saw that they were leaving, marching away in groups of two and three, the weak helping the weaker. As they disappeared around the curving shoreline, the voices of the last two, bringing up the rear far behind the others, fell faintly on her ears over the sound of the surf.

"Is it possible that we're all corrupted, Director?"

"It's possible, but we're not."

"I wish I could be sure."

"See Antonio up ahead there? What do you think of him?"

"I still can't believe it."

"He'll never be the same."

"Tell me something. What was the most unusual thing you noticed back there?"

"You must be joking, sir. Why, the way those logs were off of us suddenly—"

"Yes, of course. But I mean besides that."

"Well, I guess I was kind of preoccupied. You know, frightened and confused."

"But didn't you notice our little glitchy friend?"

"Oh, that. I'm afraid not, Director. I—I guess I was thinking mostly of survival."

"Hmmm. If I could only be sure I saw it. If only someone else saw it too."

"I'm afraid I don't follow you, sir."

"Well, damn it all, you know that Antonio tagged it with the deletion tool. Got it in the leg. That being the case, why would the anomalous little entity come back to help us—back to us—when we were trapped under those logs?"

"Well, I guess as long as we were trapped, it figured we couldn't harm it anymore.... I'm sorry, that was illogical. I'm still a little disoriented."

"Forget it. Look, you go ahead to the exit portal and prepare for logout. I'll join you in a few minutes. I think I'll go back and look around. You know. Make sure we haven't left anyone."

"No need to do that. They're all ahead of us. I've verified."

"That's my responsibility, Grace, not yours. Now go on."

As Elena lay gathering strength for the long trek back to the hub, she saw through dimming vision one of the avatars coming back along the beach. When it was nearly directly below her, she could hear it making sounds that by now had become familiar.

"Where are you?"

Elena paid little attention to her companion's actions; she was beyond understanding. She wondered what would happen when her session expired.

"We've made a terrible mistake. We—" The sounds faded in and out on Elena's perception as the avatar turned slowly and called in different directions. She watched the avatar walk over to the pile of scattered logs and peer around and under them.

"If you're hurt I'd like to help!" The twin moons were high in the sky now, and where their light broke through the swirling clouds a double shadow was cast around the avatar. With fading awareness, Elena watched the figure shake its head slowly, then walk away in the direction of the others.

Elena's eyes stared, without seeing, at the panorama before her. The beach was deserted now, and her gaze was fixed on a shimmering white square floating on the ocean. Across it, the last thing Elena ever saw, was emblazoned the word ANTONIO.
